screens.title: Working with Touched Events and Proximity Prompts
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you’ll deepen how your game notices and responds to players. We’ll make the Part. Touched event reliable by validating what actually hit your part, and we’ll stop rapid repeated triggers with simple debounce patterns so interactions feel intentional and fair. Then you’ll learn ProximityPrompt: a modern, player-friendly way to ask for deliberate interaction with an object, like opening chests or talking to NPCs. You will see concrete scripts for a damage zone that safely affects only players, a teleporter pad that respects per-player cooldowns, and a secret door that uses a ProximityPrompt to require a short hold before opening. Along the way I’ll point out common mistakes—like pausing the whole script inside an event handler—and show safer alternatives. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to choose between Touched, ClickDetector, and ProximityPrompt with reasons, and implement each pattern cleanly. Consider how each method affects player experience and server performance as you build.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will deepen three practical skills that make game interactions predictable and player-friendly. First, you will learn to interpret the argument passed to Part. Touched and reliably determine whether the colliding object belongs to a player character by checking the part’s parent and the presence of a Humanoid. This matters because without that validation you will accidentally trigger actions for falling objects or non-player models. Second, you will implement debounce logic so that standing or repeated collisions do not cause repeated effects. You’ll see a per-player timestamp table pattern that prevents rapid damage or multiple pickups. Third, you will add and configure ProximityPrompt on Parts so players receive clear, on-screen prompts to press a key and commit to an action. The prompt’s properties let you control text, required hold time, and input keys. Each objective includes short examples and a verification milestone so you can confidently test your scripts.

screens.title: What does the Touched event pass to your handler?
screens.narratorSegment: When Part. Touched fires the handler receives one argument commonly named hit or otherPart. That argument is the specific BasePart that contacted your part. It might be a limb on a player character, a small loose part, or a Physics projectile. The first step in any touch-based logic is to treat that argument as untrusted input and validate it. A practical validation sequence is: get otherPart. Parent, check for a Humanoid instance inside that parent, then use GetPlayerFromCharacter to confirm you are dealing with a player-controlled character rather than an NPC or an unrelated model. This sequence prevents false triggers when non-character parts collide with your trigger. For example, a pickup that runs when any part touches will misfire if a stray piece falls onto it. A common misconception is assuming every touch is a player; that leads to unpredictable behavior. Also, remember parts inside tools, accessories, or welded objects may have parents you must traverse. Always guard your handler with early returns if validation fails. Finally, practice the Parent → Humanoid → Player order until it becomes second nature; it will save you from many debugging headaches.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Touched Argument
Definition
The event handler receives the specific BasePart that collided. That part can originate from many sources.
Get otherPart.Parent and treat missing parent as invalid.
Check for a Humanoid with FindFirstChildOfClass.
Confirm a real Player with game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter.
Key Takeaway

Always validate the hit argument before applying game-changing effects.

Analogy & Example
Think of otherPart like a mail package dropped at your door — first check the label (parent), verify the recipient (Humanoid), then confirm the sender is the correct account (Player) before opening the contents.
Quick code pattern
-- inside a Touched handler
local character = otherPart.Parent
if not character then return end
local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
if not humanoid then return end
local player = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character)
if not player then return end
-- safe to act on humanoid or player now
Common mistake
Assuming hit is a player part; causes false activations from tools or debris.
Pro tip
Use early returns for each guard to keep handlers simple and readable.

screens.title: Validating a touch: Parent → Humanoid → Player
screens.narratorSegment: Validation is a small sequence that prevents many bugs. Start by reading the argument and retrieving its parent; parts without parents are invalid. Next, check for a Humanoid instance inside that parent. A Humanoid tells you the model behaves like a character with health and movement, which is the most common case for player-based interactions. If there is no Humanoid, treat it as a non-character collision and return. Finally, when the Humanoid exists, call GetPlayerFromCharacter to get the Player object. This step distinguishes actual human players from NPCs or scripted actors. A simple process diagram you can remember is Parent, Humanoid, Player. Implement this as early-return guards in your handler so the rest of the code assumes a valid player. A misconception is thinking Humanoid presence guarantees a Player; always confirm with GetPlayerFromCharacter if you only want to affect players. Testing tip: put print statements in each guard while developing to see which checks are passing or failing in multiplayer tests. Validating a touch: Parent → Humanoid → Player means guard your handler with parent, humanoid, then player checks so only intended actors cause effects.. In practical terms, a reliable sequence to confirm player interactions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Validation sequence
keyIdea.text: Guard your handler with Parent, Humanoid, then Player checks so only intended actors cause effects.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Validation Sequence
Step-by-step checks
1. Parent: Get otherPart.Parent. If nil, return immediately. Many stray parts have no parent.
2. Humanoid: Use FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid"). If absent, it is likely not a character.
3. Player: Call game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character). If nil, it's not a human player.
Why this order?

Each step reduces the chance of false positives and keeps event handlers safe to operate on player state.

Developer checklist
  • Use early returns for each failed guard.
  • Log which guard failed during testing to diagnose false triggers.
  • Remember tools and accessories may have parts parented differently—inspect in Explorer.
Small example (pattern)
local character = otherPart.Parent
if not character then return end
local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
if not humanoid then return end
local player = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character)
if not player then return end
-- safe to proceed
Pro tip: Use prints during testing to see which guard stops the flow.
Misconception: Humanoid alone equals a player — not always true for NPCs.

screens.title: Debounce patterns for Touched events
screens.narratorSegment: A common pitfall with Touched is many rapid firings while a part remains in contact, producing repeated damage or duplicate pickups. The safest pattern is a per-player cooldown table that stores the last action time keyed by player UserId. When the handler runs, compute the difference between os. time() and the stored time; if it's less than your cooldown, return. This pattern avoids pausing the script with task. wait inside the handler and avoids global booleans that don't scale to multiple players. The chapter example uses playersInZone[player. UserId] = os. time() and checks os. time() - lastDamageTime < COOLDOWN_TIME to guard effect application. A misconception is using a single boolean debounce; that blocks all players or fails with concurrent touches. Another wrong approach is sleeping inside the handler; that stalls the entire script thread. Test cooldowns by standing on the part and watching console prints for last-damage timestamps. This approach is efficient, simple, and works well for damage zones and teleporter pads. Debounce patterns for Touched events means use a per-player timestamp table and os.time() to guard repeated touched triggers without blocking the script.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use a per-player timestamp table and os.time() to guard repeated Touched triggers without blocking the script.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Debounce Patterns
Why debounce matters
Touched can fire many times per second while parts remain in contact. Without debounce, you get runaway effects.
  • Per-player timestamp table avoids cross-player interference.
  • os.time avoids sleeping the script and is server-safe.
  • Use UserId as the key so the table survives player name changes.
Damage zone pattern (excerpt)
-- Script inside "DamageZone"
local DAMAGE_AMOUNT = 10
local COOLDOWN_TIME = 1
local playersInZone = {}

local function onDamageZoneTouched(otherPart)
  local character = otherPart.Parent
  if not character then return end
  local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
  if not humanoid then return end
  local player = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character)
  if not player then return end

  local lastDamageTime = playersInZone[player.UserId] or 0
  if os.time() - lastDamageTime < COOLDOWN_TIME then
    return
  end

  humanoid:TakeDamage(DAMAGE_AMOUNT)
  playersInZone[player.UserId] = os.time()
end

damageZone.Touched:Connect(onDamageZoneTouched)
Pro tip: Use os.time() for server-wide consistent cooldowns.
Don't: Use task.wait inside the handler—this blocks the thread.

keyIdea.text: Use a per-player timestamp table, validate hit ownership, and update timestamps after applying effects.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Damage Zone Example
Full script (as shown in chapter)
-- Script placed inside a Part named "DamageZone"
local damageZone = script.Parent
local DAMAGE_AMOUNT = 10
local COOLDOWN_TIME = 1 -- seconds

local playersInZone = {}

local function onDamageZoneTouched(otherPart)
    local character = otherPart.Parent
    if not character then return end

    local humanoid = character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not humanoid then return end

    local player = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character)
    if not player then return end

    local lastDamageTime = playersInZone[player.UserId] or 0
    if os.time() - lastDamageTime < COOLDOWN_TIME then
        return
    end

    humanoid:TakeDamage(DAMAGE_AMOUNT)
    playersInZone[player.UserId] = os.time()

    if humanoid.Health <= 0 then
        playersInZone[player.UserId] = nil
    end
end

damageZone.Touched:Connect(onDamageZoneTouched)
Explanation & checks
  • Guard checks prevent non-player triggers and early-exit quickly.
  • Per-player timestamps avoid blocking and correctly scope cooldowns.
  • Cleaning the table on death prevents stale entries.
Common mistake: using task.wait inside the handler which pauses the whole script.
Pro tip: Use UserId as key to handle name changes safely.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Teleporter Pad
Activity steps
  1. Create TeleportPadA and TeleportPadB in Workspace, anchored and non-colliding.
  2. Insert a Script into TeleportPadA and get a reference to padB.
  3. Validate otherPart, humanoid and player in Touched handler.
  4. Find HumanoidRootPart and set its CFrame to padB.CFrame plus an upward offset.
  5. Use a teleportCooldowns table and os.time to prevent rapid teleportation.
Starter code (template)
-- Script placed inside "TeleportPadA"
local padA = script.Parent
local padB = game.Workspace:FindFirstChild("TeleportPadB")

if not padB then
    warn("TeleportPadB not found! Teleporter will not work.")
    return
end

local teleportCooldowns = {}

local function onPadATouched(otherPart)
    local character = otherPart.Parent
    local humanoid = character and character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    local player = game.Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(character)

    if humanoid and player then
        local lastTeleportTime = teleportCooldowns[player.UserId] or 0
        if os.time() - lastTeleportTime < 2 then return end

        local hrp = character:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart")
        if hrp then
            hrp.CFrame = padB.CFrame + Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)
            teleportCooldowns[player.UserId] = os.time()
            print(player.Name .. " teleported to Pad B!")
        end
    end
end

padA.Touched:Connect(onPadATouched)

screens.title: Introducing ProximityPrompt
screens.narratorSegment: ProximityPrompt is a built-in instance that gives players an in-world instruction when they approach an object. It is ideal for interactions that must be deliberate, such as opening a chest, starting dialogue, or activating complex machinery. Key properties you will set include ActionText which tells the player what pressing the key will do, and ObjectText which names the object. HoldDuration controls whether the player must hold the key for a short time, preventing accidental activation; setting it to zero makes activation immediate. You can configure KeyboardKeyCode and GamepadKeyCode to map the input. RequiresLineOfSight toggles whether the player must see the object to trigger it. The main event is Triggered, which passes the Player who activated the prompt. Unlike Touched, ProximityPrompt offers a clear visual affordance and requires a deliberate input, so it reduces accidental triggers and improves UX. Remember: ProximityPrompt is best for guided interactions rather than passive environmental effects. Introducing ProximityPrompt means use actiontext, objecttext, holdduration, and triggered to create clear, deliberate interactions.. In practical terms, what it does and which properties matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: ProximityPrompt is a built-in instance that gives players an in-world instruction when they approach an object. It is ideal for interactions that must be deliberate, such as opening a chest, starting dialogue, or activating complex machinery. Key properties you will set include ActionText which tells the player what pressing the key will do, and ObjectText which names the object. HoldDuration controls whether the player must hold the key for a short time, preventing accidental activation; setting it to zero makes activation immediate. You can configure KeyboardKeyCode and GamepadKeyCode to map the input. RequiresLineOfSight toggles whether the player must see the object to trigger it. The main event is Triggered, which passes the Player who activated the prompt. Unlike Touched, ProximityPrompt offers a clear visual affordance and requires a deliberate input, so it reduces accidental triggers and improves UX. Remember: ProximityPrompt is best for guided interactions rather than passive environmental effects. Introducing ProximityPrompt means use actiontext, objecttext, holdduration, and triggered to create clear, deliberate interactions.. In practical terms, what it does and which properties matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › ProximityPrompt
What ProximityPrompt provides
  • A visual prompt above the part when a player is nearby.
  • Configurable action and object text for clarity.
  • Optional hold duration to require a deliberate action.
  • Triggered event supplies the Player who activated it.
Important properties
ActionText: Instructional verb like "Open" or "Talk".
ObjectText: Object name shown to player, like "Chest".
HoldDuration: Seconds the key must be held before activation.
KeyboardKeyCode / GamepadKeyCode: Input bindings for activation.
RequiresLineOfSight: If true, the player must see the prompt target.
When to use:
Use ProximityPrompt when you want player agency and clear instructions for interaction.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › ProximityPrompt Triggered
Locked chest script
-- Script placed inside a Part named "LockedChest"
local chest = script.Parent
local prompt = chest:FindFirstChildOfClass("ProximityPrompt")

if not prompt then
    warn("LockedChest is missing a ProximityPrompt!")
    return
end

prompt.ActionText = "Open"
prompt.ObjectText = "Chest"
prompt.HoldDuration = 0.5
prompt.KeyboardKeyCode = Enum.KeyCode.E

local isOpen = false

local function onPromptTriggered(player)
    if isOpen then
        print("Chest is already open!")
        return
    end

    print(player.Name .. " opened the chest!")
    isOpen = true
    chest.BrickColor = BrickColor.new("Dark green")
    prompt.Enabled = false

    -- spawn loot or perform other actions
end

prompt.Triggered:Connect(onPromptTriggered)
Explanation & tips
  • Triggered gives you the Player, so no hit validation is needed.
  • Use a state variable to prevent duplicate handling while the action executes.
  • Disable the prompt for one-time interactions, or re-enable after reset if needed.
Pro tip: Use HoldDuration to reduce accidental activations for important actions.

keyIdea.title: Secret Door pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a Prompt to open a door briefly; disable prompt while open and restore state afterward.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Secret Door
Secret Door script template
-- Script placed inside "SecretDoor"
local door = script.Parent
local prompt = door:FindFirstChildOfClass("ProximityPrompt")

if not prompt then
    warn("SecretDoor is missing a ProximityPrompt!")
    return
end

prompt.ActionText = "Open"
prompt.ObjectText = "Secret Door"
prompt.KeyboardKeyCode = Enum.KeyCode.E
prompt.HoldDuration = 0.5

local isDoorOpen = false

local function onPromptTriggered(player)
    if isDoorOpen then return end

    print(player.Name .. " opened the secret door!")
    isDoorOpen = true
    prompt.Enabled = false

    door.Transparency = 1
    door.CanCollide = false

    task.wait(5)

    door.Transparency = 0
    door.CanCollide = true
    isDoorOpen = false
    prompt.Enabled = true
end

prompt.Triggered:Connect(onPromptTriggered)
Testing checklist
  • Confirm prompt shows ActionText and ObjectText correctly.
  • Press and hold to activate when HoldDuration > 0.
  • Ensure door disappears and reappears after the set time.
Pro tip: Disable the prompt while the door is open to avoid competing activations.

screens.title: Touched vs ClickDetector vs ProximityPrompt
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the correct interaction mechanism shapes player experience. Touched is best for passive, physics-driven interactions like damage zones, healing pads, or simple teleporters where proximity alone should cause an effect. ClickDetector works well when players must click a specific object—good for desktop-focused direct interactions and small buttons players expect to click. ProximityPrompt is the modern choice for guided, context-sensitive interactions that require deliberate player input; it shows a clear UI hint such as 'E to Talk' and supports hold durations and input mapping for gamepads. A useful mental model: if the action should happen automatically when touched, use Touched; if it should happen only when the player aims and clicks, use ClickDetector; and if it should be shown as a clear instruction with a key press, use ProximityPrompt. Watch out for accidental triggers with Touched and confusion with ClickDetector on small or moving targets; ProximityPrompt often avoids these UX problems by demanding intent. Always match the tool to the interaction's required level of explicit player agency. Touched vs ClickDetector vs ProximityPrompt means use touched for passive triggers, clickdetector for direct clicking, and proximityprompt for guided intentional interactions.. In practical terms, choose the right interaction for the situation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Robust scripting practices and cleanup
screens.narratorSegment: Writing robust interaction scripts means more than making the first feature work. Track per-player state rather than global booleans, because games are multiplayer and actions should not interfere across players. Avoid pausing the entire script with task. wait inside frequently-called handlers; instead use timestamp checks for debouncing. When using ProximityPrompt, keep UI clarity by setting ActionText and ObjectText and disabling prompts while actions complete. Clean up event connections when destroying objects by using Connect only when the lifetime matches or by disconnecting on object removal. Consider performance: avoid heavy work inside Touched handlers; if an expensive operation is needed, defer it to a separate coroutine or queue. For temporary state like a door being open, set clear timeouts and re-enable prompts if repeatable. Finally, provide visible feedback—color changes, prints for debugging, or simple animations—so you and players know interactions succeeded. These practices reduce bugs and make multiplayer behavior predictable. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you’ll deepen how your game notices and responds to players. We’ll make the Part. Touched event reliable by validating what actually hit your part, and we’ll stop rapid repeated triggers with simple debounce patterns so interactions feel intentional and fair. Then you’ll learn ProximityPrompt: a modern, player-friendly way to ask for deliberate interaction with an object, like opening chests or talking to NPCs. You will see concrete scripts for a damage zone that safely affects only players, a teleporter pad that respects per-player cooldowns, and a secret door that uses a ProximityPrompt to require a short hold before opening. Along the way I’ll point out common mistakes—like pausing the whole script inside an event handler—and show safer alternatives. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to choose between Touched, ClickDetector, and ProximityPrompt with reasons, and implement each pattern cleanly. Consider how each method affects player experience and server performance as you build.

In this chapter you will deepen three practical skills that make game interactions predictable and player-friendly. First, you will learn to interpret the argument passed to Part. Touched and reliably determine whether the colliding object belongs to a player character by checking the part’s parent and the presence of a Humanoid. This matters because without that validation you will accidentally trigger actions for falling objects or non-player models. Second, you will implement debounce logic so that standing or repeated collisions do not cause repeated effects. You’ll see a per-player timestamp table pattern that prevents rapid damage or multiple pickups. Third, you will add and configure ProximityPrompt on Parts so players receive clear, on-screen prompts to press a key and commit to an action. The prompt’s properties let you control text, required hold time, and input keys. Each objective includes short examples and a verification milestone so you can confidently test your scripts.

In this continuation we’ll translate objectives into verifiable steps you can test in Studio. For touch-based scripts, you will run a scenario where a player steps into a damage zone and verify their humanoid health changes only once per cooldown interval. For teleports, you will validate that the HumanoidRootPart moves to the destination and that the per-player cooldown prevents rapid re-teleportation. For prompts, you will confirm the prompt shows ActionText and ObjectText, requires a hold when set, and passes the player to the Triggered handler. Each objective includes a small mnemonic—Parent → Humanoid → Player—to remember validation order. Finally, you’ll practice a simple assessment question that asks you to pick the most robust debounce pattern from alternatives. These testing steps ensure your scripts work consistently in multiplayer scenarios and that you can diagnose common mistakes quickly.

When Part. Touched fires the handler receives one argument commonly named hit or otherPart. That argument is the specific BasePart that contacted your part. It might be a limb on a player character, a small loose part, or a Physics projectile. The first step in any touch-based logic is to treat that argument as untrusted input and validate it. A practical validation sequence is: get otherPart. Parent, check for a Humanoid instance inside that parent, then use GetPlayerFromCharacter to confirm you are dealing with a player-controlled character rather than an NPC or an unrelated model. This sequence prevents false triggers when non-character parts collide with your trigger. For example, a pickup that runs when any part touches will misfire if a stray piece falls onto it. A common misconception is assuming every touch is a player; that leads to unpredictable behavior. Also, remember parts inside tools, accessories, or welded objects may have parents you must traverse. Always guard your handler with early returns if validation fails. Finally, practice the Parent → Humanoid → Player order until it becomes second nature; it will save you from many debugging headaches.

Validation is a small sequence that prevents many bugs. Start by reading the argument and retrieving its parent; parts without parents are invalid. Next, check for a Humanoid instance inside that parent. A Humanoid tells you the model behaves like a character with health and movement, which is the most common case for player-based interactions. If there is no Humanoid, treat it as a non-character collision and return. Finally, when the Humanoid exists, call GetPlayerFromCharacter to get the Player object. This step distinguishes actual human players from NPCs or scripted actors. A simple process diagram you can remember is Parent, Humanoid, Player. Implement this as early-return guards in your handler so the rest of the code assumes a valid player. A misconception is thinking Humanoid presence guarantees a Player; always confirm with GetPlayerFromCharacter if you only want to affect players. Testing tip: put print statements in each guard while developing to see which checks are passing or failing in multiplayer tests. ProximityPrompt is a built-in instance that gives players an in-world instruction when they approach an object. Choosing the correct interaction mechanism shapes player experience. Touched is best for passive, physics-driven interactions like damage zones, healing pads, or simple teleporters where proximity alone should cause an effect. ClickDetector works well when players must click a specific object—good for desktop-focused direct interactions and small buttons players expect to click. ProximityPrompt is the modern choice for guided, context-sensitive interactions that require deliberate player input; it shows a clear UI hint such as 'E to Talk' and supports hold durations and input mapping for gamepads. A useful mental model: if the action should happen automatically when touched, use Touched; if it should happen only when the player aims and clicks, use ClickDetector; and if it should be shown as a clear instruction with a key press, use ProximityPrompt. Watch out for accidental triggers with Touched and confusion with ClickDetector on small or moving targets; ProximityPrompt often avoids these UX problems by demanding intent. Always match the tool to the interaction's required level of explicit player agency.
